cards.title: AI video ad generation: aspect ratio, prompt description, extensions
cards.summary: How to generate a UGC-style talking-head video ad with an AI video tool, including prompt structure and extending a cut-off clip.
cards.use_when: You need a first batch of paid-social ad creatives (TikTok/Meta feed) for a product page or offer and are generating them with an AI avatar tool rather than shooting.
steps: Before generating, set the aspect ratio to match the placement you'll run in (vertical 9:16 for TikTok/in-feed).

Write a description that specifies three things: the model's posture/action, the product prop, and the talking points. Example format from the source: 'have the model sitting like she is while holding the charger and talking about how great it is for charging her phone and other devices.'
Let the tool generate (source notes ~2–5 minutes per render). Budget the tool's credits per render — the base image-to-video generation cost one credit in the source's example.

Review the output for an abrupt cut-off. If the script is truncated, use the tool's Extend button (or find Extend under presets) and describe what the continuation should say, e.g. additional feature walkthrough.
Extend deliberately: the source used extend to go from ~12 seconds to ~19 additional seconds so the avatar could cover more features. Remove the extension if it dilutes the hook.
Download the finished file and upload it as a manual ad creative with your CTA and destination URL.
caveats: Credit costs and render times are tool- and plan-specific and change; verify the current interface and pricing before planning a batch.
Extensions can hurt performance if the extra seconds dilute the opening hook — evaluate the full clip, not just completion.

cards.title: Swipe competitor hooks and re-voice them for your product
cards.summary: Download a winning competitor or platform hook, upload it to an AI ad tool, and regenerate it with your product inserted to test hook variations cheaply.
cards.use_when: You have product and offer ready but are stuck on ad angles, or you want to test multiple opening hooks for the same PDP/offer without reshooting.
steps: Build a swipe file: use a platform that lets you filter top-performing TikTok (or cross-platform) videos to find proven hooks — the source used Foreplay, which is a paid tool with other options available.
Pick a hook whose format is transferable to your category (e.g. 'My For You page convinced me to buy something again, but this one is actually worth the hype' works for almost any physical product).
Download that video and upload it into your AI video tool as the reference.
Give the tool a short instruction naming your product: the source's example was simply 'Can you talk about my product Premier Supplements?' — the AI preserved the hook and swapped the product.
Generate and review: in the source's run, the output reproduced the hook and inserted the presenter's product, at a lower credit cost (~0.4 credits) than a from-scratch render.
Repeat with multiple hooks against the same product to build a hook-test set for your campaign's creative split test.
Use this as a hook-testing machine, not a final asset: run the variations as separate ads so platform data tells you which hook wins.
caveats: The source demonstrates hook copying on a made-up brand; results are illustrative, not a performance promise.
Reproducing another brand's script verbatim risks IP/brand issues — use the hook structure with your own claims and verify your product claims are compliant.
AI may paraphrase or drop parts of the reference; check the output for accurate product claims.

cards.title: Choose the right AI video model for your ad by constraint
cards.summary: Model selection for AI ad video: pick based on which constraint matters most — realism, exact length, or resolution.
cards.use_when: You are generating product or UGC-style ad videos and need to decide which generation model to spend credits on for a given spot length or placement.
steps: If realism and 'does this look like a real person using the product' are the priority, the source prefers Sora 2 / Sora 2 Pro and reports using it for most ad outputs, using a product image plus a short description.
If you need an exact duration (every second between ~3s and 15s), use Kling 3.0 — this matters when your spot must hit a defined length for a placement or a multi-scene edit.
If you need high resolution (up to 4K), V0 3.1 offers that, but the source reports its cinematic, artistic style often doesn't match UGC-ad aesthetics and uses it least for ads.
For Sora 2, plan around fixed length options (4, 8, or 12 seconds) and 1080p; if your ad concept requires other lengths, either use Kling or extend the clip.
When prompting, attach a product image so the model renders the actual item, and give a plain-language ad brief (source example prompt: 'make me a UGC ad for a company that sells office chairs').
Allow for post-editing: the source notes Sora 2 sometimes cuts off the video at an odd angle, requiring trimming after generation.
caveats: Model availability, resolution and duration limits change quickly — verify current options in the tool before building a production plan.
Model preference here is the presenter's opinion based on their testing, not a benchmark; run your own A/B between models on the same product.

cards.title: Motion control and presets to skip
cards.summary: Use motion-transfer to animate a still of a person/product into an existing motion, and avoid the unboxing POV preset because of hand artifacts.
cards.use_when: You want a scroll-stopping format (person reactivating a product, showing a device in motion) without a shoot, or you are deciding which AI presets are worth spending credits on.
steps: For motion transfer, upload (1) a reference video containing the motion you want, and (2) a still image of the person you want performing it. The tool transfers the motion onto your image.
Source example workflow: a clip of a woman dancing was used as the motion reference, and an AI-generated image of a man in an office was the subject; the output made the man perform the same motion.
Adapt the format to commerce: instead of dancing, capture the motion of holding up a product, demonstrating a device, or reacting to unboxing — the motion source can be any clip.
This is a lower-priority format: the source says they rarely use it, so treat it as a novelty format to test, not a core creative.
Avoid the 'unboxing POV' preset for product unboxing ads — the source reports the hands (e.g. crumpling paper) look visibly wrong and it isn't worth the credits.
Instead, prompt Sora 2 to 'make a video of this being unboxed' when you need unboxing content, and treat that output as the testable version.
caveats: Motion transfer adds a step and may produce artifacts on hands and props — inspect closely before setting spend.
Preset quality changes with model updates; the unboxing-POV warning is a snapshot of the presenter's testing, so re-evaluate periodically.

cards.title: Pick the TikTok ad objective that matches your goal (and why Sales is the default)
cards.summary: TikTok campaign objectives map to funnel stages, but optimizing for Sales is the source's default because it trains delivery toward purchases.
cards.use_when: You are setting up a new TikTok Ads Manager campaign for a product and need to decide what to optimize the account toward before spending budget.
steps: Treat the objective list as a funnel: Awareness/Reach sits at the top (max reach, no optimization toward a page view or sale), Consideration (Traffic, Video Views, Community Interactions) sits in the middle, and Conversion (App Promotion, Lead Generation, Sales) sits at the bottom.
Choose Sales for most ecommerce campaigns, because the goal is a purchase and the algorithm optimizes delivery toward the conversion you've selected.
Only use Reach when the explicit goal is spreading awareness (e.g. a launch) and you accept poor ROAS on that spend.
Consider Community Interactions only for growing a profile's engagement/followers, not for driving a product purchase.
Confirm your TikTok pixel is installed and firing before you optimize toward a purchase — you cannot optimize for a conversion event the pixel isn't reporting.

Inside Sales, you also choose a destination (TikTok Shop vs Website — manual, Smart+, or search). Expect different available options across objectives: the source notes features like creative split testing are not available for every objective, and placements and billing events can differ per objective.
Start with the manual website campaign rather than the recommended Smart+ campaign, and treat Smart+ as a parallel test later: the source reports mixed results between the two in their testing.
caveats: If the pixel isn't set up, the purchase optimization will not function; fix the pixel first.
Objective availability, Smart+ recommendations, and per-objective feature sets are TikTok product specifics that change — verify in the current Ads Manager.
The 'always use Sales' stance is the presenter's opinion for ecommerce; campaigns with pure awareness goals are a legitimate exception.

cards.title: Manual vs Smart+ campaign and the product catalog setting
cards.summary: Choose manual for control, disable the campaign catalog to avoid showing unintended products under your video, and label campaigns by audience for later reporting.
cards.use_when: You are configuring a new TikTok Sales campaign and deciding whether to use Smart+, whether to show a product catalog under the video, and how to name campaigns.
steps: Start with the manual campaign instead of the TikTok-recommended Smart+; the source reports mixed results between them and prefers manual first, then testing Smart+ alongside it.

Turn the campaign catalog OFF for a first campaign. It pulls images from your product catalog and displays products under the video, which can surface products you didn't intend to promote and add visual clutter. The source keeps it unchecked so only the video and the one product you want are shown.
Name the campaign by audience purpose — the source uses 'Prospecting' to mark cold-audience campaigns — so you can read performance at a glance.
Only check the Special Categories box if you are advertising housing, employment, or credit; otherwise leave it.
Leave Create Split Test unchecked for now unless you have a specific structured test planned.

Decide campaign budget optimization (CBO) here: leaving it off lets you budget at the ad-group level so each audience gets a predictable share (e.g. $25 each across four ad groups), which is what the source recommends for new accounts.
caveats: The source expects mixed manual-vs-Smart+ results, so don't assume one is universally superior.
The catalog setting may be useful for some use cases (e.g. shops with many SKUs); the recommendation to turn it off is specifically for getting-started campaigns.

cards.title: Campaign budget optimization: off for testing, on for scaling
cards.summary: Leave CBO off when testing audiences so each ad group gets a defined budget, then enable it when scaling to let TikTok allocate toward what already works.
cards.use_when: You are deciding between campaign-level and ad-group-level budget allocation for a TikTok campaign, particularly when comparing broad vs interest audiences.
steps: Understand the mechanism: with CBO on, you set one budget at the campaign level and TikTok distributes it across ad groups however it favors — e.g. $80/$10/$5/$5 out of four groups — with no control from you.
With CBO off, set budget at the ad-group level (the source's term: ad group budget optimization) so each ad group receives an even, predictable amount (e.g. $25 each) and audience tests stay clean.
For new accounts, keep CBO off so you can see which audiences perform and manually move budget toward winners.
Once you've identified winners, switch to CBO for scaling — the source uses it to direct money toward proven ad groups.
If CBO is on, the campaign asks for a daily budget; if off, the daily budget field appears at the ad-group level. Set it there.
Keep the structure shallow: the source generally does not recommend more than four ad groups inside a campaign.
caveats: The >4-ad-group guidance is a practical heuristic from the presenter's experience, not a platform rule.
Switching CBO on re-allocates spend in ways you don't control, so don't use it while you still need clean per-audience comparisons.

cards.title: Budget recommendations for TikTok: CPA multiples vs TikTok's 10x rule
cards.summary: TikTok recommends 10x CPA daily budget; the source prefers 2x current CPA (or $50 if unknown, $20 minimum) and frames budgets around escaping the learning phase.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much daily budget to put behind a new TikTok conversion campaign for a product.
steps: Know the platform constraint: TikTok requires a $20/day minimum. Attempting less is rejected in the interface.
Know the platform's recommendation so you can judge it: TikTok suggests 10x your current CPA (e.g. $10 CPA -> $100/day; $40 CPA -> $400/day).

The source does not like the 10x rule for most advertisers. Instead, budget at 2x your current cost per acquisition: a $10 CPA implies a $20/day budget; a $20 CPA on other platforms implies ~$40/day here.
If you don't know your CPA, start around $50/day as a test budget.
If budget forces you to $20/day, proceed but expect a long learning phase.

Understand the learning phase: performance fluctuates while the system finds the best users, and volatility typically settles after 25 campaign results or seven days. Aim to accumulate the 25 results inside the seven-day window if budget allows.

Set the start time, keep campaigns running continuously rather than scheduling short flights, keep day-parting on all day, and leave the optional target CPA and attribution windows untouched on a new account.
caveats: The 25-results/7-day learning phase is TikTok's described mechanism; the source's 2x-CPA budget is their own alternative to TikTok's 10x advice, not a platform rule.
The 10x recommendation makes 2x-CPA budgets hard for high-CPA products — expect slower learning if you underfund.
Leave target CPA blank until you have real data; setting it without data can constrain delivery.

cards.title: TikTok cost expectations and the one lever that moves them
cards.summary: Typical TikTok cost ranges (CPM, CPC, CPV) and the factors that shift them, with creative quality named as the dominant driver.
cards.use_when: You are setting CPA and ROAS targets for a TikTok ad plan or diagnosing why your costs are above/below plan.
steps: Use these as rough planning ranges rather than promises: CPM roughly $3–$10 per thousand impressions; CPC roughly $0.17–$1.00; cost per view roughly $0.01–$0.07.
Expect CPA to vary widely depending on product price, category and many other factors — don't apply a single benchmark across categories.

Understand the cost drivers the source lists: creative quality of the ad (good UGC-style ads get cheaper CPMs), audience targeting (broader is cheaper), industry competition (beauty supplements are more expensive), and seasonality (Q4 holiday costs rise).
Treat creative quality as the biggest lever: the source says the better the ad, the cheaper your views, and reports seeing this repeatedly across accounts.
Apply this to decisions: if CPMs are high, test a new hook (see the hook-repurposing workflow) before expanding targeting or raising budget.
Plan seasonal buys ahead of Q4 — raise budget expectations rather than assuming the same CPA holds.
caveats: These ranges are presented as typical, not guaranteed; the source notes having seen both lower and much higher costs, especially on poor ads.
CPM/CPC/CPV bands vary by country, currency and account history — treat them as directional.

cards.title: Audience targeting: start broad, layer interest testing later
cards.summary: Broad targeting is the source's default because the algorithm finds buyers; add interest/behavior ad groups only when budget allows a clean comparison.
cards.use_when: You are configuring TikTok ad-group targeting (demographics, interests, spending power, devices) for a product campaign.
steps: Start with broad targeting — TikTok itself states broad is best for most advertisers, and the source agrees: with a strong ad, the algorithm finds the right people. The source reports testing this multiple times and finding broad works well.
For a $20/day budget, use one campaign (Prospecting) with one broad ad group containing three ad creatives. Once a winner emerges, move it to a new campaign and scale.

For a larger budget, duplicate the ad group and keep identical settings except the audience: one broad vs one interest/behavior, running the same three ads in each, so you can compare audiences on equal footing.
Keep the same ads in both ad groups: the source duplicated the ad group with its ads so the only variable is targeting.

For interest targeting, search by category keyword (e.g. 'swimsuit') and add 3–5 relevant interests, purchase intentions, video interactions, creator interactions or hashtags. Ignore 'audience narrow' warnings if the reach figure is healthy — the source's example showed ~7 million people while still flagged as narrow.
Leave spending power on 'All' unless you sell luxury. The source tested narrowing to high spenders and found it limits delivery without improving results.

Leave household income on 'All' — the source doubts the platform knows true household income well. Leave devices on all, and leave placements automatic, then check placement data later; TikTok placement is generally the strongest performer.
caveats: Broad vs interest is presented as a budget-dependent test, not a universal rule — the source also admits a personal bias toward granular targeting that the algorithm tends to beat.
Interest targeting significantly narrows reach; only worth it if you have the budget to run proper ($20/day per ad group) comparisons.
Demographic filters like spending power are the presenter's tested opinion, not platform-verified performance data.

cards.title: Build one ad group, then duplicate it for multiple audiences
cards.summary: Set up one ad group with all creatives first, then duplicate the ad group to create audience variants rather than rebuilding ads each time.
cards.use_when: You are structuring a TikTok campaign that needs separate broad and interest (or demographic) ad groups using the same creative set.
steps: Create one ad group and build all the ads (3–5 creative) inside it first — if you plan to run 3–5 ads, creating them before duplication saves you recreating them in each copy.
Create the ad group with a temporary name, then name it after targeting is set (e.g. 'broad USA' with language, age, gender adjustments as needed).
Publish, then go to the ad-group level in the campaign view and use Duplicate -> duplicate the ad group into the existing campaign.

In the duplicate, change only the audience: add interest/behavior targeting (e.g. swimsuit-related interests), then rename to something like 'interest USA' so broad vs interest is unambiguous in reporting.
Keep all other settings identical between the two ad groups so the audience is the only variable.
To add more creatives later, duplicate the ad inside the ad group and use the update button on the copy to swap in a different video or TikTok post.
Keep at most ~4 ad groups per campaign as a working guideline.
caveats: Duplicating before all creatives are built forces you to update each copy manually — build ads first.
Parallel ad groups each need their own minimum daily budget (~$20/day in the source's examples), so this structure multiplies spend.

cards.title: Set up TikTok in-feed ad creative: CTA, music, and the ad-library checkbox
cards.summary: Practical creative-level settings for a TikTok ad: use multiple CTAs for testing, decide on music sharing, and uncheck the ad-library box.
cards.use_when: You are in the ad creative step of a TikTok campaign, uploading a video or spark post, and setting the CTA, URL, and visibility options.
steps: In the ad creative section you have two source options: upload a video from your computer, or grab an existing TikTok post from a linked account to run as a spark ad (you need your TikTok account linked to the ads account for this).
Add as many appropriate call-to-action options as possible so TikTok can test which gets the most clicks for that specific video — but make sure each CTA actually makes sense for your product.
Leave music sharing OFF: this option lets others use the sound from your ad, which the source leaves disabled.
Leave product tagging off unless you have TikTok Shop set up and want to tag specific products; the source covers shop product tagging in a later module.
Add your destination URL; TikTok appends UTM parameters for you.
Confirm you have the rights to any music in the ad.
Uncheck the option that places your ad in the TikTok ad library — the source stresses keeping this unchecked so your ads do not appear in the library.
Publish all, then duplicate the ad if you want additional creative variations inside the ad group.
caveats: Ad library visibility, music sharing and CTA list options are platform UI features that change — verify current naming and defaults in Ads Manager.
Running an existing post as a spark ad requires the profile-to-ad-account link; without it, that option won't be available.
This card covers in-feed; search campaigns and TikTok Shop setups differ.

cards.title: Keyword research for TikTok search ads with the Keyword Planner
cards.summary: Use TikTok's Keyword Planner to build a 20–50 keyword list filtered by competition and volume, then save it as a plan to upload into a search campaign.
cards.use_when: You want to run TikTok search ads (users typing queries inside TikTok) for a product and need a keyword list with realistic CPC and volume expectations.
steps: In TikTok Ads Manager, go to Tools -> Keyword Planner (verify current menu location, as platform UI changes).
Enter your product or category (e.g. 'swimsuits'), set the target area (e.g. United States), and run Discover.
Read the output columns: keyword, average monthly searches, three-month change, year-over-year change, competition level, and estimated low/high CPC.

Filter by low competition first and add any relevant terms — the source finds cheaper average clicks on low-competition terms, though volume is smaller and many results may be irrelevant or in other languages.
Then re-run with all competition levels, sort by monthly search volume, and add the relevant high-volume terms.
Aim for roughly 20–50 keywords. Source example: this produced ~52,000 total monthly search volume, which they judged enough to build a campaign on.
Save the plan with a specific name (e.g. 'swimsuits') — saving is required so you can pull the list into the campaign later.
Use this research to sanity-check whether search ads are worth running for the product at all: if volume is negligible, skip the campaign.
caveats: Keyword Planner data is directional; the source notes some results were irrelevant (other languages, unrelated terms) and had to be filtered manually.
The 20–50 keyword / 52k volume example is the presenter's working heuristic, not a validated threshold.
Tool location and columns can change; check the current interface.

cards.title: Build a TikTok search campaign and pick match types
cards.summary: Set up a TikTok search campaign from a saved keyword plan, choose phrase match as the middle ground, and disable automated keywords.
cards.use_when: You are launching a TikTok search ad campaign targeting people actively searching for your product terms.
steps: Create a new campaign with the Sales objective and select the search campaign type (instead of manual or Smart+). Reference your saved keyword plan.
Reuse your pixel and conversion settings: website destination, conversion event = purchase. Leave target CPA blank if you don't know it.

Load your keywords from the saved keyword plan. If you skip pre-research, you can search inside the campaign, but the source finds the in-campaign view gives fewer options — do the research beforehand.

Understand the three match types: broad maximizes reach by matching relevant searches; phrase shows ads on searches with the same meaning as your keyword; exact shows ads only for searches containing your exact phrase in order and limits reach most.
The source's default: start with phrase match as the middle ground — you'll appear for related terms like 'modest swimwear' but not wildly unrelated queries.
If you must only appear for specific terms (e.g. black swimsuit or red swimsuit), use exact match and separate ad groups per keyword theme, accepting reduced reach.
Turn automated keywords OFF at launch so you know exactly what your ads show up for; the source treats it as an optional later test.

Set daily budget (minimum $20), start/end times, US + 18+ demographics as appropriate, and note placements are limited to TikTok search results for this campaign type. Allow user comments. Build the ad with a destination URL and a video or spark post, then publish.
caveats: Exact match will meaningfully cut reach; only use when a term is high-volume and highly relevant.
Automated keywords can be tested later, but at launch the source prefers full control over query matching.
Search campaign placement is constrained to search results — this is not a feed placement.

cards.title: Mine the search term report and add negative keywords
cards.summary: After launching a search campaign, review the search terms your ads actually appeared for and exclude unwanted queries with negative keywords.
cards.use_when: You have a TikTok search campaign running and need to protect spend from irrelevant queries that don't match product intent.
steps: Click into the search campaign, go to the ad group level, and open View Data.
Open the Search tab to see the search term report — the actual queries your ads were shown against.
Review the list closely, as the source recommends doing this after a couple of days of running, to confirm you're showing up for terms that match your brand and product.
Where you see irrelevant queries, use the report's option to add them as negative keywords so your ad no longer appears for them.
Repeat this review periodically — it is described as very important when running search campaigns, because broad/phrase matching will pull in tangents over time.
If you have keyword-specific product angles (e.g. black swimsuit vs red swimsuit), use this data to decide whether to split them into separate ad groups with their own creative.
caveats: Search term reports need volume before they're informative; the source suggests checking after a couple of days, not immediately at launch.
Match type changes (e.g. switching broad to phrase) affect the quality of the terms you'll later need to exclude.

cards.title: Spark ads: requirements and the organic-first six-step workflow
cards.summary: Run Spark ads by posting creative organically first, waiting 5–7 days to prove it, then amplifying the winners with paid budget.
cards.use_when: You want to amplify organic TikTok content (your own or a creator's) as a paid ad rather than treating paid and organic as separate tracks.
steps: Confirm the prerequisites: a TikTok Ads account (set up in the course), a TikTok profile if the Spark ad runs from your own account, and the profile linked to the ads account. If using influencers, obtain an ad authorization code from them (optional but required for creator posts).
Step 1 — create three or more videos yourself or have influencers create them.
Step 2 — post them to your TikTok account, or have influencers post to theirs.

Step 3 — wait five to seven days for the post to reach its full organic potential; roughly a week is the typical life cycle of a new TikTok post, and you can usually tell within the first two days whether it's starting to get organic traction.
Step 4 onward — do not step in immediately: the source's rationale is that you don't want to spend ad budget amplifying a post that can still earn free organic impressions.
After the organic window, run the winning posts as Spark ads to scale the reach that already proved itself.
Two ways to run them: boost one of your own existing posts, or boost a creator's post using their authorization code.
caveats: The 5–7 day wait is the presenter's tested workflow, not a platform requirement; faster campaigns can still boost earlier.
You must have the profile-to-ad-account link and, for creators, an authorization code — without them the Spark ad can't be created.
This is a lead-in to paid amplification and the source covers the full Spark ad build in a later module; verify current linking and authorization steps in Ads Manager.
